children: By Shaina Mishkin
The midterm election results gave an immediate boost to stocks in most corners of the housing industry, from Rocket, a mortgage company, to home builder D.R. Horton.
Investors apparently were making the calculation that Democratic wins in the Senate and House could lead to changes in tariffs and other policies that would lower home building costs.

That hope won't go far unless mortgage rates begin to come down, and the overall housing market improves. In fact, housing stocks were largely lower in midday trading Thursday as the major indexes tanked.

The election results, meanwhile, were perceived as detrimental to the case for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac common shares, which hinges on the companies' long-awaited release from government conservatorship.
With a blue Congress, "we think [privatizing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac] potentially goes down in how much of a priority it is," KBW analyst Bose George tells Barron's.

The midterm results don't necessarily change the mechanics of removing Fannie and Freddie — which are often referred to as the "government-sponsored enterprises," or GSEs, for short — from conservatorship, says KBW's George.
"You don't need congress for GSE privatization," he says.
But disagreements between the Republican administration and a Democratic House and Senate on other issues could push untangling Fannie Mae and Freddie Macs' futures down on the agenda, he says.

Investors appeared to feel the same: Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae common shares, which trade in OTC Markets, closed 12.7% and 13.7% lower, respectively, on Wednesday. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Housing Finance Agency, the companies' conservator, did not respond to requests for comment.

Both continued to slide Thursday morning: Fannie Mae was down 12.5% in morning trading, while Freddie Mac was 13.1% lower. Both are on track for their largest two-day declines in over a year, according to Dow Jones Market Data, with the former on track for its largest such decline since the two days ended Aug. 21, 2023, and the latter on pace for its worst two-day stretch since Jan. 15-16, 2025.
The stocks' two-day declines stood in contrast to a housing sector that largely rallied on the results of the midterm election, but gave away some of their postelection gains on Thursday.

Home builders big and small, from the market capitalization leader D.R. Horton to the $1.2 billion Dream Finders Homes, were moving lower in Thursday trading. D.R. Horton was down 0.8% Thursday after rising 8.1% Wednesday, while Dream Finders dropped 2.1% following its 26.8% Wednesday gain, according to FactSet data.

The same held for brokerages, mortgage originators, and housing technology companies. The brokerages Compass and AGNT, which owns eXp, were both down 6.2% Thursday after closing 7.7% and 8.9% higher, respectively, on Wednesday.
The mortgage company Rocket was down 1.2% after closing 8.7% higher Wednesday, while United Wholesale Mortgage was down 4.4% after closing 6.3% higher the day prior.

The housing technology company Zillow was down 9% in Thursday trading after reporting disappointing third-quarter financial results and weak guidance Wednesday night. The decline nearly erased the stock's 9.4% gain one day prior.

The rally in housing stocks was, in part, the same post-midterms relief rally that pushed much of the broader market higher on Wednesday — though hopes that a blue Congress would curtail tariffs and wind down the war in Iran likely gave builders an extra boost.
"Democratic control of Congress raises the potential for lower tariffs, which we estimate represent $7,500 of additional cost per home," UBS analyst John Lovallo wrote in a Wednesday note.

Other potential changes, including the possibility of passing legislation supporting the housing sector, a reduction in tensions in the Middle East, and an easing in immigration policy, would represent "incremental tailwinds for housing under a Democratic Congress," he wrote.

Investors in housing stocks will take any hope of home-building or buying cost relief they can get — particularly as they size up the housing market's prospects for spring, which is typically when homebuying demand ramps up. Builder margins are under pressure as the housing market churns toward its fourth straight year of relatively high costs and fewer sales. To keep homes selling, builders often offer buyers incentives or cut prices at the expense of their margins on home sales.

Mortgage rates — which have remained lodged above 7% since mid-September — are one of the main drivers of recent deterioration. Fixed 30-year mortgage rates are largely driven by fluctuations in the 10-year Treasury yield, which has risen 0.739 percentage point this year as of Wednesday afternoon, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
A reversal in tariff policy is unlikely, even with a blue Congress, Barron's previously reported, while bonds yields have not yet shown signs of a strong retreat.
Thursday's reversal in housing stocks shows that investors will need more than just hope for an improvement in costs.
